title: Dedicated Throughput Tiers (Beta) — GTM Enablement Deck (Draft)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Dedicated Throughput Tiers (Beta): Standard / Performance / Premium
Internal GTM Enablement (Draft)

Speaker notes:
- This deck is for Sales/CS/Support enablement. Not customer-facing.
- Goal: align what we promise, how we measure it, what we sell, and what we enforce.


Slide 2 — Agenda
- Why we’re doing this now
- What is “throughput” (and what it is not)
- Tier overview (Standard / Performance / Premium)
- Hardware shapes + regional availability (what we can actually deliver)
- Burst + overload behavior (what customers experience)
- Packaging guidance + qualification
- Customer examples (Northpeak AI, Helio Search)
- FAQ + objection handling
- Beta rollout + next steps

Speaker notes:
- Expect most questions around: “tokens/sec vs req/sec”, “mixed prompt sizes”, “what happens if they spike”, and “remedies/credits”.


Slide 3 — Why now (customer + internal pain)
Customer pain:
- Dedicated customers buy “predictable capacity” but experience variability and unclear commitments.
- Customers want commitments that map to their application SLOs and procurement language.

Internal pain:
- Sales proposals, SRE operations, and runtime behavior aren’t aligned on a single measurable guarantee.
- We’ve been over-indexing on bespoke guarantees → exceptions → escalations.

What changes with tiers:
- One definition of throughput.
- Enforceable guardrails (admission control) to protect commitments.
- Packaging language + contract references that don’t require custom edits per deal.

Speaker notes:
- Use this slide to set context: we’re not reducing what we offer; we’re making it reliable and repeatable.


Slide 4 — Executive summary (what to remember)
- Dedicated now has 3 throughput tiers with explicit assumptions + measurement standard.
- Primary guarantee is sustained OUTPUT tokens/sec (not “requests/sec”), measured over a defined window.
- Tiers map to hardware shapes and operational policy (burst allowance, overload mode, maintenance expectations).
- If a customer asks for a bespoke number: default is to move them up a tier; exceptions require pricing uplift + SRE/Infra signoff.

Speaker notes:
- Keep it simple: the big change is clarity + enforcement.


Slide 5 — Definitions: what is “throughput” (Dedicated)
Throughput (Dedicated) = sustained output tokens per second delivered by the deployment
Measurement (high level):
- Aggregated at deployment level
- Windowed rate (not instantaneous)
- Exclusions: warm-up, planned maintenance, and customer-induced errors

What it is NOT:
- Not a per-request latency guarantee (latency guardrails exist but are secondary)
- Not a fixed “requests/sec” across all prompt sizes
- Not a promise that we will never throttle (throttling is the enforcement mechanism)

Speaker notes:
- Phrase it as: “we guarantee a floor on sustained output tokens/sec under stated assumptions; if you try to exceed it, you’ll see predictable throttling rather than unpredictable degradation.”


Slide 6 — Why tokens/sec and not requests/sec
- Requests vary (prompt length, output length, streaming vs non-streaming, tool calls).
- Tokens/sec correlates better with GPU resource consumption and fleet planning.
- Requests/sec can be supplied as a *derived* estimate for a specific workload profile, but not the contract metric.

Speaker notes:
- If asked: “Can you give req/sec?” → Yes, via sizing exercise and workload profile; but the guarantee is tokens/sec.


Slide 7 — Measurement assumptions (talk track)
The guarantee assumes:
- Model is pinned (or within an allowed model family for that tier)
- Context length distribution stays within agreed envelope (we’ll help define it)
- Concurrency stays within recommended range for the shape
- Customer integration follows best practices (stream consumption, retry behavior)

Common exclusions / carve-outs:
- Planned maintenance window (communicated)
- Customer-induced errors: timeouts from client, broken connections, invalid requests
- Force majeure / cloud provider region outage (standard SLA language)

Speaker notes:
- Don’t over-legalize. Keep it practical: “We’ll show you the dashboard; if you exceed the envelope, we’ll throttle and tell you why.”


Slide 8 — Tier overview (one slide)
Standard
- Baseline predictable throughput for stable production workloads
- Moderate burst allowance
- Standard regional availability

Performance
- Higher sustained throughput and tighter tail-latency guardrails
- Higher burst allowance + faster mitigation response
- Availability subject to shape supply in-region

Premium
- Highest sustained throughput + strongest operational posture
- Strictest isolation and most conservative maintenance coordination
- Limited availability (supply-constrained shapes/regions)

Speaker notes:
- Avoid promising a specific GPU in the abstract; position tiers as “outcomes + policy”, backed by shapes.


Slide 9 — Tier matrix (draft; final numbers in tier sheet)
Standard (draft anchors)
- Designed for: steady workloads, moderate concurrency, cost-sensitive
- Guarantee: sustained output tokens/sec floor (per deployment)
- Burst: allowed up to a defined ceiling for a defined duration (throttling beyond)

Performance (draft anchors)
- Designed for: spiky workloads, higher concurrency, customer-facing latency sensitivity
- Guarantee: higher sustained output tokens/sec floor
- Burst: higher ceiling; overload mode prefers throttling over latency collapse

Premium (draft anchors)
- Designed for: strict predictability + procurement-driven SLA language
- Guarantee: highest floor + strongest operational commitments
- Burst: controlled; coordinated capacity planning

Speaker notes:
- This deck intentionally avoids hard numbers because they vary by model/shape. Use the Tier Matrix v1 sheet in deal cycles.


Slide 10 — Hardware shapes (how tiers translate to fleet)
Supported shape families (examples; region-dependent):
- L4 pool (single-node): good $/token for smaller models / embeddings / rerank; generally Standard
- A100 pool (single- or multi-node depending): Performance default for many chat workloads
- H100 pool (premium supply): Premium / select Performance cases for highest throughput and headroom

Notes:
- MIG vs no-MIG: tier eligibility depends on isolation requirements and perf consistency
- NVLink / multi-node: used where needed to hit perf targets for large models

Speaker notes:
- If customer asks “Can I pick H100?” → We sell a tier + region + model. Shape preference is a constraint request, not the package itself.


Slide 11 — Regional availability (set expectations)
- Tier availability is constrained by GPU supply (especially Premium)
- Standard: broad availability across primary NA/EU regions
- Performance: available in selected regions; confirm with Capacity Ops before committing start dates
- Premium: limited regions + longer lead times; requires capacity reservation and explicit launch plan

Speaker notes:
- Key GTM behavior change: no more ‘yes’ on the call without checking the capacity channel.


Slide 12 — Burst policy (what customers experience)
Definitions:
- Sustained guarantee = floor we commit to deliver (under assumptions)
- Burst = temporary allowance above sustained baseline

What happens during burst:
- Requests are accepted up to a tier-specific burst ceiling
- If sustained load persists beyond burst, admission control activates

What the customer sees when above tier:
- Predictable throttling / 429s (or queued behavior where configured)
- Clear metrics: throttled_request_rate, queue_depth, effective_tokens_per_sec

Speaker notes:
- Use “guardrails prevent noisy-neighbor behavior (even within a dedicated deployment) caused by self-induced overload patterns and protects latency.”


Slide 13 — Overload mode (why it’s good)
Overload mode goals:
- Protect committed throughput and prevent cascading latency collapse
- Provide deterministic behavior under pressure

Overload mode behaviors (by tier):
- Standard: earlier throttling; best-effort latency
- Performance: higher headroom; prefers controlled queueing + throttling
- Premium: strict adherence to committed envelope; coordinated mitigation

Speaker notes:
- Don’t let customers interpret throttling as “outage.” It’s policy enforcement to preserve SLO.


Slide 14 — Observability + reporting (what we show customers)
Customer-visible (in Console / exports):
- Current throughput vs guarantee (time series)
- Effective output tokens/sec (windowed)
- Throttling rate and reasons
- Queue depth / saturation indicators
- Deployment metadata: tier, region, model, shape class

Internal (SRE/Infra):
- Alerting on sustained under-delivery and abnormal throttling
- Error budget tracking by tier

Speaker notes:
- Good moment to reassure: “you’ll have the same charts we do” (with customer-friendly filtering).


Slide 15 — Packaging: what’s included (tier differentiation)
Common across all Dedicated tiers:
- Dedicated GPU pool, data isolation
- Model pinning + controlled rollouts
- Basic dashboarding and export
- Standard support processes

Performance add-ons (included):
- Higher burst allowance
- Tighter guardrail tuning + faster response targets

Premium add-ons (included):
- Strongest operational posture (coordination on changes, most conservative maintenance handling)
- Priority capacity planning process
- SLA/contract language alignment (standard clauses, fewer bespoke edits)

Speaker notes:
- Keep it aligned with what Product/SRE have agreed; no “we can do anything” promises.


Slide 16 — Qualification: which tier should I sell?
Ask these questions:
1) What is the target user experience? (latency sensitivity vs batch processing)
2) What is your concurrency and traffic shape? (steady vs spiky)
3) What is your prompt + output length distribution? (p50/p95)
4) What region(s) and timeline? (capacity constraints)
5) Do you need contractual throughput language / remedies?

Routing:
- If they care about procurement-grade guarantees → Performance or Premium
- If they need maximum headroom and predictable scaling under spikes → Performance
- If they are cost-sensitive with stable load → Standard

Speaker notes:
- The fastest path is mapping their workload profile to an envelope.


Slide 17 — How to talk about mixed prompt sizes (script)
Customer question: “We have mixed prompt sizes; what does the guarantee mean?”
Suggested answer:
- “The guarantee is in output tokens/sec and assumes a context-length envelope. Mixed prompts are fine as long as your distribution stays within that envelope.”
- “We’ll help you define p50/p95 prompt lengths and concurrency. Then we’ll size shape + tier to ensure the sustained floor.”
- “If the distribution shifts (e.g., many more long-context requests), you’ll see it in dashboards and we may recommend moving tiers or adjusting capacity.”

Speaker notes:
- Offer to run a benchmark scenario matching their distribution (avoid ad-hoc promises).


Slide 18 — Customer example #1: Northpeak AI (prospect)
Context:
- AI-native product; peak hour spikes and user-visible latency sensitivity
- Region preference: US (multi-region later)
- Key ask: “How do we know we won’t degrade during peaks?”

Recommended path:
- Start Performance tier in US region
- Define envelope: concurrency target + prompt length distribution
- Include burst policy + overload mode explanation in proposal

Proof points to use:
- Customer-visible throughput vs guarantee dashboard
- Admission control prevents latency collapse; predictable throttling beyond ceiling

Speaker notes:
- Keep this framed as “less surprise” rather than “more hardware.”


Slide 19 — Customer example #2: Helio Search (enterprise)
Context:
- Enterprise procurement + auditability; wants clear SLA language and reporting
- Comparing Dedicated vs self-host; concerns about ‘shared’ behavior and ambiguous commitments

Recommended path:
- Premium tier (if region capacity allows) OR Performance with contract addendum (if Premium unavailable)
- Emphasize: defined measurement standard + remedies + carve-outs
- Provide: reporting export + escalation path

Speaker notes:
- For enterprise: lead with measurability + governance, not just speed.


Slide 20 — Competitive framing (internal only)
What customers often compare:
- “Dedicated GPU instances + self-managed runtime”
- Other managed endpoints with opaque throttling

Redwood Dedicated tiers differentiate by:
- Measurable sustained throughput guarantee (not marketing ‘capacity’)
- Enforced policies (burst + overload) that preserve predictability
- Unified observability + exportable reporting
- Deployment flexibility (hosted/dedicated/private alignment)

Speaker notes:
- Avoid naming competitors in customer calls unless necessary.


Slide 21 — Objections + responses
Objection: “Why can’t you guarantee requests/sec?”
- Response: requests are not normalized; tokens/sec is the accurate capacity metric. We can translate to req/sec for your workload profile.

Objection: “Throttling is unacceptable.”
- Response: throttling is how we preserve the guarantee and avoid runaway latency. We’ll size tier/burst to your peak needs.

Objection: “We need the highest numbers; can you do a bespoke commitment?”
- Response: usually solved by moving to Performance/Premium. Exceptions require formal review due to reliability and fleet constraints.

Speaker notes:
- Repeat: “predictable behavior” and “dashboard evidence.”


Slide 22 — Contract/SLA positioning (guardrails)
What Sales can say (safe):
- “Throughput guarantee is defined by our published measurement standard.”
- “Remedies/credits apply when we under-deliver under the agreed envelope (excluding carve-outs).”

What Sales should not do:
- Don’t paste custom token/sec numbers into free-form order forms
- Don’t promise specific GPU types without capacity confirmation
- Don’t promise ‘no throttling’ or ‘unlimited burst’

Process:
- Use approved clause pack for tier language
- Route deviations via Legal + Product DRI

Speaker notes:
- Point to the internal ‘approved language’ snippets once Legal finalizes.


Slide 23 — Discounting + exceptions (how to avoid fire drills)
Default guidance:
- Discount guardrails depend on tier and term; follow pricing guidance doc
- If customer asks for higher guarantee than tier supports:
  1) try next tier
  2) increase reserved capacity
  3) if still required → exceptions process

Exceptions require:
- Product signoff (Dedicated DRI)
- SRE/Infra capacity feasibility
- Pricing uplift to cover risk + opportunity cost

Speaker notes:
- The goal is to prevent “hero deals” that break SLO posture.


Slide 24 — Beta rollout plan (internal)
Phased approach:
- Week 0: internal enablement (this deck + cheat sheet + FAQ)
- Week 1–2: pilot 3–5 accounts (mix of startup + enterprise)
- Week 3–4: publish tier pages + standard proposal language
- Week 4+: broader availability by region/shape readiness

Pilot candidates (initial):
- Northpeak AI (Performance)
- Helio Search (Premium/Performance depending on region capacity)

Speaker notes:
- Beta means: controlled commitments, limited regions, tight feedback loop.


Slide 25 — Support / CS readiness (what happens when customers complain)
If customer reports “throughput is low”:
- Confirm tier + model + region + timestamp window
- Pull dashboard: throughput vs guarantee + throttling rate + queue depth
- Check for overload mode / client disconnect patterns
- Escalate with required artifacts (template)

Escalation routing:
- Runtime (scheduler / decode) if effective tokens/sec drops without saturation
- Infra if GPU saturation / node issues
- SRE if SLO breach suspected

Speaker notes:
- Reassure Sales: we’ll have a consistent playbook to reduce back-and-forth.


Slide 26 — FAQ (rapid fire)
Q: Can customers burst indefinitely?
A: No. Burst is time/ceiling bounded by tier. Beyond that, admission control triggers.

Q: Do we guarantee latency too?
A: Latency guardrails exist, but Dedicated tier primary guarantee is throughput. Latency depends heavily on prompt/output lengths.

Q: Can a customer change tiers later?
A: Yes, subject to region/shape availability and contract terms; requires coordination for capacity planning.

Q: What about model upgrades?
A: Model changes can change throughput; customers can pin versions. Changes are governed by rollout policy and may require re-benchmarking.

Q: Is the guarantee per node or per deployment?
A: Per deployment (as defined in the measurement standard).

Speaker notes:
- Keep answers short, route details to the internal FAQ doc once published.


Slide 27 — Appendix: What’s still being finalized (as of 2025-03-03)
- Final tier thresholds per model family + shape baseline safety factors
- Region-by-region availability table for Performance/Premium
- Final approved order form language snippets
- Console UI: where tier and throughput status is surfaced

Speaker notes:
- Encourage reps to sell what’s approved; don’t invent. For anything unclear: ask in #sales + tag Dedicated DRI.


Slide 28 — Call to action
- Use tiers in new Dedicated proposals starting this month (beta)
- For active opportunities: schedule a 20-min sizing session (Sales + Solutions + Product)
- Send feedback: what’s confusing, what customers push back on, missing collateral

Owner + channel:
- Enablement owner: Stephanie Nguyen
- Product DRI: Lauren Bishop
- Escalations: route via #dedicated-throughput-slo (internal)

Speaker notes:
- Keep the feedback loop tight; we’ll revise deck weekly during beta.
